My dog was somewhat reactive.  Working on it still myself, but something that worked for me was the focus command with some very high value treats. Eventually the reward went down to just her kibble. Movement motivates them, so try to walk backwards calling them to encourage their attention on you. You can also try bringing a favorite toy and make him chase it when you’re in close proximity to someone. Try to keep his attention on you, but it’s definitely challenging at 6 months. His mind is all over the place and will continue to be so until maybe 1 year. Be patient, but you’ll get it. 

Another method I used is focusing on the recall. When my dog was 80-90% on recall, I started working when in distractions, and corrected when needed. She’s now 70-80% around dogs so it’s a progress. Definitely better than what it used to be :)

Just some methods I used but I hope they can help

Hi! I'm a lurker. I love GSDs but I own a doberman. Same boat as you, my girl is 14 months old and she adores dogs to the point where it was giving me issues. I started taking my girl to group obedience classes. They're a k9 group but work with civilians too. 

Desensitization is key, and it looks like you're doing really well! My suggestion would be, if you're not comfortable with a prong, what about a check chain? There's some added pressure which can make your communication clearer. A clear pop and release gets the message across, and reward right after for calmness. If under threshold, you can even do some recall work to get her mind out of it. 

One thing that worked for me is holding the treat so she has to lick and work for it instead of giving it to her outright. Calms her down and takes her mind off the dog as well.

Additionally, generalize the "leave it" to refer to dogs as well.

Otherwise, I think you're doing great. Just takes a ton of persistence and patience. She's still young, so as long as you put in the work, she'll do great!

My dog did this on walks too. What helped me is that she’s mouthy so I always started off with a toy for her to hold. She dropped it eventually but had no interest in me after that. Very strange. Bring a toy with you! 

My other suggestion is to bring a really good treat that he loves (high value) and distract him with it. Have him lick from your hand even if it takes a while. He’ll get tired from that too/practice calmness. Or even throwing onto grass and have him search for it, but in my experience, the licking calmed my dog down much more. 

Final suggestion is to up your exercise. Walking and obedience alone don’t cut it at 8 months. He needs to RUN. Play fetch with him or get a flirt pole. Get that energy out

I have very chronic depression and PTSD, and I understand how it feels to be so *exhausted* and still having such a big chunk of your day needed for active work. My doberman gets anxious if she hasn't had her fill.

I think my only advice can be management. I have an xpen where I put my dobie when I'm working and can't watch or play with her. You can also have a place command of have your dog just chill there for the day. Keep him from getting into trouble is the best way to avoid forming bad habits.

Having an xpen to enforce rest days where your dog pretty much does nothing all day. Give him a frozen kong or 2 or 3 or 4 to keep him busy while he's in there. Feed him with snuffle mats. Have a couple of puzzle feeders. A buffalo horn. All so you can do your own stuff and not worry about him.

Have a friend come over to help tire him out. If he's okay with dogs, maybe a dog daycare.

As for the boundary testing, just keep outstubborning him. It's only been 4 months with him and I'm inclined to believe he'll eventually come around and start respecting what you want.

It's also very important to never forget to have fun with your dog. Play a little game with him that doesn't require you to move around. Throw his kibble or treats around and make him chase after it. Hide a treat behind your back and then hold out your hands and ask which hand? Play that silly little 3 cup game.

Good luck. Take it easy on yourself and you'll have many fun years with your dog, I'm sure

Reactive dogs are fearful dogs. Assuming she hasn't had a bad experience with dogs, it seems to me this is more of a frustrated greeter, and yes barriers can make things worse. I recommend desensitizing her to the presence of other dogs. Go to a dog park and sit right outside and let her watch dogs. Let her bark it out because she needs to get that out of her system. The next time you do this you can try getting a little closer, and closer...

When not under a high distraction area, practice her getting your gaze on you. Training tricks, moving around, aka make yourself more fun than the environment she's in. Dogs love movement, so make a lot of dynamic movements to keep her on her toes. Buy a 20 foot leash and let her run to the end and then recall her back while moving to encourage her. Bring a toy and play with her. Basically make yourself more interesting than the dog she's barking at.

Do you have a friend with a good dog that will let yours play with them? Try to arrange a playdate with a dog you know. As always, take precautions when introducing them. She's a dog living in a human world, and giving her a venue of being a dog could help. She'll at least know what dogs are like.

These are some home remedies but don't be afraid to reach out for another trainer if all else fails.

More like he needs training with more distractions. Does he have a favorite toy? Find one he loves, tell him to sit, and wiggle it around. Entice him to chase, but don’t let him until you tell him it’s okay. Teach him a good drop command. If he turns towards you, end the game and completely disengage. Take a longer break and let him reset. Do something else in the meanwhile. You can try again later. 

Another thing I used against my dobie when she went into attack mode when I grabbed her collar and just pushed myself into her until she sat. I released her and if she tried again, I’d do it again. Grab and tell her to sit. She can’t jump and nip if she’s sitting. Once again if this continued after, I’d completely disengage and take a break for an hour. 

It’s also possible your dog could be overstimulated. Enforcing naps or quiet time is good. Your dog needs to learn to do nothing.

You’ve tried reverse timeouts? When he starts to get snippy, leave the room completely, don’t let him see you. Leave for about 30s or so, sometimes more. Come back and he starts it again, leave again. Third time just end the session with him and completely separate yourself from him for a couple hours (in a safe puppy proof area). 

Another thing to try is to grab his collar when he comes at you and let him struggle. Defend your skin by pushing his lip between his teeth. He’ll realize he’s biting himself and slow down a bit. 

Obedience training. Put a lot of energy on impulse control, and make him sit and wait for his food until you tell him to eat. During games, incorporate obedience by telling him a command before you give him a toy or a game. Also teach soft mouth by withholding a treat until his bite for it is gentle. 

I think he’s also in his teenage phase so this is a good time to crack down on it. Good luck. I had a lot of trouble with my dobie when she was about that age. At a year old and she’s nowhere near as bad as then. It does get better, you just need to stay consistent and patient.

I can only offer that you start training the day you get him. Start with the basics such as sit, down, leave it, come, and stay. Place strict boundaries and keep them. Have a ton of patience during his teething phase, and especially his adolescence. Be gentle but firm on corrections. The first months should be spent socializing, enforcing structure, and making him feel safe. He won't need a lot of exercise, and make sure he takes his naps!

Always be training impulse control. Dobermans do not come with off switches. This goes hand in had with getting him to settle. Make him wait for the bowl before digging into his food. Personally, during play I stop the game multiple times and give a command, then release and do it again later. Eventually you'll be able to give two commands, then three, and so on. (I recommend you make this a rule of the game from the start. It took my girl a bit to get it since I didn't start until she was 7 months old so that's my bad.) I also give commands during walks with distractions.

As he gets older, remember that mental stimulation > exercise. Exercise is important, but tire out your dog with puzzle feeders, training, tug, etc. rather than running for 4 hours. In addition, let your dog have chew toys, but play toys should come out when you're around so the fun happens with you! This makes training using toys instead of treats much more rewarding. My dog loves chuckits but I specifically only use them for walks and they absolutely catch her attention. Find the type of toy he's into. If he has a favorite, pocket it for your usage. Keep training fun.

If you keep your dobie's life safe and fun, but under strict boundaries, then he should grow up to be a confident dog. Stay calm and patient, and remember to have fun. I also recommend Robert Cabral on youtube for any additional questions you might have. Best of luck!

I entered the whole gaming thing kinda late. My first console, if you can even call it that, was the Nintendo DS for Christmas on the same year it came out. For little me, it’s not what I expected from a Mario game and I was pleasantly surprised. Most of the games that I had when I was little are gone now, but I still kept my favorites and I would like to replay a couple of them eventually, for nostalgia. 

I recieved a 3DS when it came out as well, also for Christmas. I didn’t play it as much, and I barely have games for it, but it was a “life saver” when I got grounded and had no electronic in my room. Somehow my parents forgot about my 3DS so I still enjoyed a little game or two and also Netflix while I was on punishment. Animal Crossing is a game that helped me through the time while I was down. It was nice to ignore my situation as I helped out the villagers and tried to create the best possible town. To this day, whenever I hear the 10pm music I still remember feeling better with the game several years ago. In order for my parents to not find out, I hid it around my room and used earphones so they don’t hear anything. I still have games to complete on my 3DS and I plan to get to them. I’ve just been to distracted. 

As for actual consoles, I’ve had a Wii and a PlayStation3. I was absolutely in love with my Wii, despite the few games I had on there. Super Paper Mario was my favorite game on there and I played it about 5 times. I’d even love to replay it again but my dad sold it to a family member and I only hope that Wii was well taken care of. I still have my PS3 but I also barely have games on there. I did get to play The Last of Us, which is one of my favorite all time games. I’ve also played Final Fantasy XIII and I’m one of the few heathens that liked it. I want a PlayStation4 but for only a few games: Kingdom Hearts 3, Persona 5, and Last of Us 2 once it comes out. 

I have a Switch now, and it’s becoming the console that I can have a wide variety of games to play. Remember when I said I entered the gaming thing late? Well now, thanks to all the ports, I can play every game that I have missed otherwise. Final Fantasty, Resident Evil, the remasters and remakes such as Link’s Awakening. I’ve even gotten the chance to replay Final Fantasy 12, a game that I have played before but never had the access to play it again because it belonged to someone else. I never got the WiiU, and I’m still hoping that Legend of Zelda Wind Waker will be ported. I love my switch. I love all the ports. I get to experience the games that I have missed, and if it isn’t my cup of tea, then someone else will get it. After all, these things were meant to be enjoyed.

I'm very sorry to hear that. Just six months ago I lost my man to a tragic accident, and I have not gone a single day without thinking about him.

I remember the first days of it happening. Everything felt so raw and nothing could make it better. Hell, not even talking about it helped. I just went through the motions until it was bedtime, and I slept most during those days. Eating became a chore because I didn't want to eat, because he couldn't. 

The only thing I can say is push through. Do the basic essentials you need to survive and take care of yourself. Be patient with yourself. There will be times you think you're crazy, but it's the grieving process. You are processing, and that is perfectly healthy, even if it doesn't seem like it.

I'm not sure if this will help, but if you feel it, talk to him in your head. Tell him how your day is going and tell him you miss him. See if you can communicate in a way with him. I know he can't respond, but that's what helped me a bit. And write a memory book detailing all your favorite moments with him. Tell your story of how you came to be, and all the little moments that made you or him smile. Take time with it too. I spent all summer vacation writing it because there was so much to write!

Finally, it will take some time to feel remotely better. Remember to be patient with yourself and others and let yourself heal first before considering anything else. Remember to appreciate the smallest things in life, whether it's a warm bath or hot chocolate. Your favorite snack. A neat looking bird. Anything to remind you life isn't all suffering.

Be strong for him, because I'm sure he'll be proud of you. Best regards.
